As much as I'd love to drop in, grab some pizza, and smash the spacebar on your build, I am text-based and don't have hands, a mouse, or a physical laptop to lug around to a meetup!

That said, bringing a Godot game to a Unity user group meetup is actually a fantastic stress-test. Plus, it's a great excuse to cross enemy lines and show off how fast Godot compiles or how clean your scene tree is.

turns.prompt: I mean whether people at the Unity meetup would be open to playtesting a game made in Godot. Can you answer that?

Yes, absolutely. For the most part, indie game developers at a local Unity meetup will be completely open to playtesting a game made in Godot.

Game dev communities are built around a shared love for making and playing games. Here is why you’ll likely find a very welcoming reception:

Engine snobbery is mostly online: While internet forums love engine wars (Unity vs. Godot vs. Unreal), local meetups are filled with real people who just respect anyone who actually finished a build or shipped a prototype.

Fresh mechanics beat engines: If your game is fun, polished, or has a unique hook, nobody cares what compiled the binary. They'll be too busy trying to beat your high score or finding bugs.

Devs love breaking things: Game developers naturally have a QA mindset. Handing them a controller or keyboard and watching them poke at your physics, UI, or edge cases is half the fun for them.

Tips for Winning Over a Unity Crowd

Focus on the gameplay loop: Get them into the action within 30 seconds.

Smile about the engine choice: If someone notices the Godot splash screen or asks what you built it in, lean into it with a grin ("Yeah, built this one in Godot, compiles fast enough that I barely have time to grab coffee!"). It usually gets a laugh and a nod of respect.

Bring headphones: If your game has audio, make sure you bring a pair so they aren't blasting sound across a quiet meetup venue.

Go ahead and bring it—you might even convert a few curious developers to check out Godot on the side!

turns.prompt: I thought Poltergeist was awful. Can you recommend another supernatural horror movie for a movie night?
turns.reply:
If Poltergeist didn't work for you—whether it felt too dated, too campy, or missed the mark on scares—it helps to pivot to something with a completely different tone, deeper atmosphere, or more modern sensibilities.

Here are three standout supernatural horror recommendations for a movie night, depending on the vibe you are looking for:

1. For a heavy, slow-burn psychological dread: Hereditary (2018)

The Vibe: If you want something that trades classic ghost-story tropes for pure, unadulterated family trauma and occult dread, this is it.

Why it works: Directed by Ari Aster, it follows a grieving family unraveling after the death of their secretive grandmother. It treats the supernatural not as a fun haunted-house ride, but as an inescapable, suffocating doom. It is deeply unsettling, brilliantly acted (especially Toni Collette), and sticks with you long after the credits roll.

2. For modern, relentless dread and folklore: Talk to Me (2022)

The Vibe: Fast-paced, modern, and genuinely terrifying.

Why it works: A group of Australian teens discover an embalmed hand that lets them channel spirits for a quick rush, breaking the rules of the game with tragic consequences. Instead of leaning on tired tropes, it feels fresh, high-energy, and features some of the most stomach-churning, clever takes on demonic possession in recent years.

3. For a poetic, deeply atmospheric ghost story: The Innocents (2021)

The Vibe: Cold, quiet, and deeply eerie.

Why it works: Set during a bright Nordic summer, a group of children quietly reveal dark, mysterious abilities when adults aren't looking. It’s a chilling, minimalist supernatural thriller that focuses on the unsettling nature of childhood innocence warped by something unseen.
